hints: Focus on what the area under a Boltzmann curve means, since it always represents the same total number of particles.
Remember that heating gives the average molecule more energy, so the whole distribution must spread out to the right and flatten.
Connect that flatter, wider shape to the area past $E_a$, which tells you how many molecules can now react.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the curve shows**

Think of the curve as sharing out energy among one mole of gas. The total area underneath never changes because the number of molecules stays the same.

Total particles = area under curve = constant

**Apply the effect of higher temperature**

At higher $T$, more molecules have higher energy, so the most probable energy shifts right. To keep the same total area, the curve must spread out and the peak P must drop down.

$$\text{higher } T \rightarrow \text{broader curve, lower peak, shifted right}$$

**Check molecules with $E > E_a$**

$E_a$ is fixed for the reaction. Because the tail stretches further to the right, a much larger fraction of the area is now beyond $E_a$. That is why rate increases sharply with temperature.

options.A: Incorrect. The peak does not get higher on heating, and the number able to react does not fall. This reverses the temperature effect.
options.B: Half right but half wrong. It is true that more molecules exceed $E_a$, but the peak P gets lower, not higher, because the same total area is spread over a wider energy range.
options.C: Incorrect. The peak does get lower, but fewer molecules exceeding $E_a$ would mean a slower rate. Heating increases the fraction with $E > E_a$, so the rate increases.
options.D: Correct. Higher temperature flattens and broadens the distribution, so peak P is lower to conserve total area, while the tail beyond $E_a$ grows and many more molecules have $E > E_a$.
